titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State

div.head: 402. Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State
div.p: 2802. Subject: (C) Discussion with President Stroessner on U.S-Paraguayan relations.

2. Summary: The Ambassador met May 18 with President Stroessner. An exchange on problems in our bilateral relations stemming from human rights problems in Paraguay dominated the discussion. Stroessner was stung at the decision not to permit the visiting U.S. Army band and parachute team to March in the national day parade. He questioned whether the USG, with all its problems, really cared about this, or about the closure of ABC Color, which, as the Ambassador explained, prompted us to curtail the band’s activities in Paraguay. The Ambassador stressed the importance the U.S. attached to the ABC problem and told the President that it would continue to affect our bilateral relations. They also exchanged views on the recent abortive visit by the Americas watch group, with the Ambassador stressing concern over the Paraguayan handling of the incident and Stroessner confirming assurances by other members of his government that the group could return to Paraguay if it wanted but would have to abide by Paraguayan laws including customs inspection. End summary.

3. The Ambassador met with President Stroessner May 18. In the course of a long conversation the two discussed strains in U.S.-Paraguayan relations which have arisen primarily as a result of recent human rights developments in Paraguay, and the U.S. reactions thereto. It was apparent that the President was most upset about the decision not to permit the visiting U.S. Army band and parachute team to march in the national day parade on May 15. He returned to this subject several times.

4. Stroessner argued that the U.S. had its hands full with problems all over the world—from the Persian Gulf to relations with China (over which he chided the U.S. for the apparent warmth of relations with the PRC). No one in the
U.S. or the U.S. Government, he insisted, would have known or cared about the participation of the band in Paraguay’s National Day parade. Thus, he could not understand why this had been cancelled.

5. The President took the occasion to point to the participation by his “good friends” the Brazilians, who brought in two warships—whose crews marched in the parade—and sent a group of Mirage fighters to overfly the parade route. They also presented the Paraguayan Air Force with two reconditioned C–47 aircraft.

6. The Ambassador responded that the USG decision was made in reaction to the closure of ABC Color. He emphasized that it was his choice, not something forced on him by the Embassy staff (this to counter an assertion the President raised several times). Moreover, the Department fully endorsed the decision, although some in Washington suggested stronger measures.

7. The Ambassador noted that there had been strenuous efforts by certain members of the Paraguayan Government to turn the decision around but that this was not possible, given the importance we attached to the “ABC” incident. This led the President to request that in the future the Embassy deal on such matters with Foreign Minister Saldivar, and not with Conrado Pappalardo.

8. Continuing on the “ABC” matter, the President complained about the statement issued by the Embassy in the immediate wake of the closure. Stroessner argued that he had consulted with the leadership of his party and the government and that they were unanimous in recommending closure of the paper in order to protect “the welfare and security of the Paraguayan people.” “ABC’s” owner, Aldo Zuccolillo, he
insisted, couldn’t be controlled, and he had to be stopped for the good of the country. Again he argued that the U.S., with all its problems around the world, could not possibly care much about what happened to a newspaper in Paraguay and complained about U.S. “interference” in this matter.

9. The Ambassador responded that as far as the U.S. was concerned the “ABC” affair was not finished. He emphasized that the GOP’s action would continue to affect our bilateral relations, and that it would certainly affect the way in which the U.S. Congress would look upon future cooperation with Paraguay. The congressional reaction to the “ABC” closure, he noted, had only begun.

10. The Ambassador also underlined once again our concern over the handling of the recent visit by the Americas watch group, and our satisfaction at the GOP’s decision to invite them to return. He emphasized the stature of the organizations which the group represented, and that the members of the group were serious people who were well-connected and respected within the U.S. and abroad. He urged that the GOP look upon such a visit as an opportunity, not a threat. The President repeated the assurances given by others that the group could return to Paraguay if it wanted to, but insisted that they would have to abide by Paraguayan laws if they did. He asked that the Embassy continue to discuss such matters related to human rights cases with Interior Minister Montanaro.

11. Throughout the meeting President Stroessner was animated, affable and alert, and he showed no signs whatever of any problems with his health. While he was clearly concerned over problems in our relations, and particularly upset over the band incident, his manner was friendly
throughout. While we doubt that he fully comprehends why we have reacted so strongly to the “ABC” closure, the band incident does appear to have brought home to him that the U.S. does attach considerable importance to human rights problems in Paraguay.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840328–0066. Confidential; Priority. Sent for information to Buenos Aires.

In telegram 3688 from Asuncion, September 1, 1983 the Embassy reported on Davis’ August 30, 1983 meeting with Stroessner who “went into a serious and long discussion of why the USG and the members of Congress could not judge his government and country on their many good points instead of basing the decisions on isolated detentions of troublemakers and repression of media trying to cause trouble for his country.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830505–0227) In telegram 5039 from Asuncion, November 2, 1983 the Embassy wrote: “During week of October 24th, three meetings with Foreign Minister, Defense Minister and the President mainly concentrated on their displeasure and speeches concerning press reports on human rights statements of Asst. Secretary Abrams and Congressmen Michels before congressional committees.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830643–0987) See “Our Human Rights Policy Has Been a Force for Good Throughout the Southern Cone,” American Foreign Policy Current Documents, 1983, pp. 1426–1434.

In telegram 1846 from Asuncion, March 22, the Embassy reported: “The Paraguayan Government closed down the nation’s leading newspaper, ABC Color, the morning of March 22, for an indefinite period.” Additionally, the Embassy included a proposed statement in response to the closure to be delivered from the Embassy and the Department, stating in part: “The Government of the United States has been encouraged by a number of positive steps taken by the Government of Paraguay since December 1983. However, we deeply deplore the closure of ‘ABC Color,’ which represents a serious violation of the principal of freedom of the press. The Government of the United States is firmly committed to the principal of freedom of the press, which is recognized by all democratic governments as one of the necessary conditions for the flourishing of democracy. We hope to see a reopening of ABC Color—without restrictions—at the earliest possible moment. The Government of the United States will continue to follow this event with great interest and concern.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840189–0259)

In telegram 94234 to Asuncion, March 31, the Department wrote: “We agree the GOP closure of ABC Color and arrest of owner/publisher is a development that requires strong response from USG. Our public statement was intended to accomplish that objective.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840211–0633) In telegram 101954 to Asuncion, April 7, the Department reported that Kilday had delivered a note to Martínez Mendieta on April 6 stating: “We deeply deplore the closure of ABC Color as a serious violation of the principle of freedom of the press, which is an essential condition of democracy. In the spirit of friendship that has characterized relations between our two countries, the Department of State urges that the Government of Paraguay reconsider this action, which can only prejudice Paraguay’s standing in the international community.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840229–0127)
